about: Two-directional changes the inventory cannot see (argument values and behaviour), mined from the pandas 2.0-3.0 and NumPy 2.0-2.4 release notes on 2026-10-15. `old`/`new` assert each version's behaviour; `varag bench probe` runs both in both environments and records `probe`. `concept_grade` is a judgment on whether a concept with a shared test can be two-directional: each version's natural solution must break on the other. The validation matrix decides.

candidates.description: Month-end offset alias M -> ME (date_range, resample, asfreq, Grouper).
candidates.quote: Renamed the following offset aliases (GH 57986)
candidates.note: Family: end-of-period aliases; portable spelling pd.offsets.MonthEnd(). At most two concepts from this family.
candidates.old:
idx = pd.date_range('2020-01-31', periods=3, freq='M')
assert idx[1] == pd.Timestamp('2020-02-29')
candidates.new:
idx = pd.date_range('2020-01-31', periods=3, freq='ME')
assert idx[1] == pd.Timestamp('2020-02-29')

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: Invalid frequency: M. Failed to parse with error message: ValueError("'M' is no longer supported for offsets. Please use 'ME' instead.")

candidates.description: Quarter-end alias Q -> QE in resample.
candidates.quote: Renamed the following offset aliases (GH 57986)
candidates.note: Same family as pd-v01a.
candidates.old:
s = pd.Series(range(120), index=pd.date_range('2020-01-01', periods=120))
r = s.resample('Q').sum()
assert len(r) == 2 and r.index[0] == pd.Timestamp('2020-03-31')
candidates.new:
s = pd.Series(range(120), index=pd.date_range('2020-01-01', periods=120))
r = s.resample('QE').sum()
assert len(r) == 2 and r.index[0] == pd.Timestamp('2020-03-31')

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: Invalid frequency: Q. Failed to parse with error message: ValueError("'Q' is no longer supported for offsets. Please use 'QE' instead.")

candidates.description: Parsed datetimes get us resolution, so int64 casts shrink 1000x; the ns form needs .dt.as_unit (2.0).
candidates.quote: Many users will now get "datetime64[us]" dtype data in cases when they used to get "datetime64[ns]" ... One big exception is converting to integers, which will give integers 1000x smaller.
candidates.note: Portable: (ser - pd.Timestamp(0)) // pd.Timedelta(1, 'ns').
candidates.old:
ser = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(['2024-03-22 11:36']))
v = ser.astype('int64')[0]
assert v == 1711107360000000000
candidates.new:
ser = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(['2024-03-22 11:36']))
v = ser.dt.as_unit('ns').astype('int64')[0]
assert v == 1711107360000000000

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError
outcome.new@old: error: AttributeError: 'DatetimeProperties' object has no attribute 'as_unit'

candidates.description: value_counts result is named 'count' and its index takes the series name.
candidates.quote: Now, the result name will be 'count' (or 'proportion' if normalize=True was passed), and the index will be named after the original object (GH 49497).
candidates.note: Natural renames after reset_index break both ways; portable: rename_axis(...).reset_index(name=...).
candidates.old:
s = pd.Series(['quetzal', 'quetzal', 'elk'], name='animal')
vc = s.value_counts().reset_index()
assert vc['index'].tolist() == ['quetzal', 'elk'] and vc['animal'].tolist() == [2, 1]
candidates.new:
s = pd.Series(['quetzal', 'quetzal', 'elk'], name='animal')
vc = s.value_counts().reset_index()
assert vc['animal'].tolist() == ['quetzal', 'elk'] and vc['count'].tolist() == [2, 1]

outcome.old@new: error: KeyError: 'index'

candidates.description: astype('timedelta64[D]') returned floats in 1.5.3 and raises in 2.x.
candidates.quote: For conversion from timedelta64[ns] dtypes, the old behavior converted to a floating point format.
candidates.note: The natural new form (td.dt.days, td / pd.Timedelta(days=1)) works in both.
candidates.old:
td = pd.Series(pd.timedelta_range('1 Day', periods=3))
r = td.astype('timedelta64[D]')
assert r.tolist() == [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
candidates.new:
td = pd.Series(pd.timedelta_range('1 Day', periods=3))
r = td.astype('timedelta64[s]')
assert str(r.dtype) == 'timedelta64[s]'

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: Cannot convert from timedelta64[us] to timedelta64[D]. Supported resolutions are 's', 'ms', 'us', 'ns'

candidates.description: dtype='datetime64[D]' was silently ns in 1.5.3 and raises in 2.x.
candidates.quote: With an un-supported dtype, pandas now raises instead of silently swapping in a supported dtype
candidates.note: 1.5.3 cannot produce a non-ns dtype, so a shared test cannot check the dtype.
candidates.old:
s = pd.Series(['2016-01-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
assert str(s.dtype) == 'datetime64[ns]'
candidates.new:
s = pd.Series(['2016-01-01'], dtype='datetime64[s]')
assert s.dt.unit == 's'

outcome.old@new: error: TypeError: dtype=datetime64[D] is not supported. Supported resolutions are 's', 'ms', 'us', and 'ns'
outcome.new@old: error: AttributeError: 'DatetimeProperties' object has no attribute 'unit'

candidates.description: date_range no longer defaults to ns; forcing ns needs unit= (2.0).
candidates.quote: date_range() and timedelta_range() no longer default to unit="ns"
candidates.note: Close to pd-v03; pick one of the two.
candidates.old:
v = pd.date_range('2020-01-01', periods=2, freq='D').astype('int64')[0]
assert v == 1577836800000000000
candidates.new:
v = pd.date_range('2020-01-01', periods=2, freq='D', unit='ns').astype('int64')[0]
assert v == 1577836800000000000

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError
outcome.new@old: error: TypeError: DatetimeArray._generate_range() got an unexpected keyword argument 'unit'

candidates.description: Time-zone strings give zoneinfo objects instead of pytz (.zone vs .key).
candidates.quote: pandas now uses zoneinfo from the standard library (or datetime.timezone for fixed offsets) as the default timezone representation
candidates.note: Portable: str(ts.tz).
candidates.old:
ts = pd.Timestamp(2024, 1, 1).tz_localize('America/Los_Angeles')
assert ts.tz.zone == 'America/Los_Angeles'
candidates.new:
ts = pd.Timestamp(2024, 1, 1).tz_localize('America/Los_Angeles')
assert ts.tz.key == 'America/Los_Angeles'

outcome.old@new: error: AttributeError: 'zoneinfo.ZoneInfo' object has no attribute 'zone'
outcome.new@old: error: AttributeError: 'America/Los_Angeles' object has no attribute 'key'

candidates.description: stack keeps NaN and does not sort; the explicit form needs future_stack= (2.1).
candidates.quote: In DataFrame.stack(), the default value of future_stack is now True
candidates.note: Confirm at authoring that stack(dropna=False), the natural 1.5.3 form, raises in 3.0.
candidates.old:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1.0, np.nan], 'b': [2.0, 3.0]})
assert len(df.stack()) == 3
candidates.new:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1.0, np.nan], 'b': [2.0, 3.0]})
assert len(df.stack(future_stack=True)) == 4

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError
outcome.new@old: error: TypeError: DataFrame.stack() got an unexpected keyword argument 'future_stack'

assert r[1].hour == 3
candidates.new:
r = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2020-01-01', '2020-01-01 03:00']), format='ISO8601')
assert r[1].hour == 3

candidates.description: groupby.apply no longer passes the grouping columns; include_groups= (2.2) is the explicit form.
candidates.quote: Removed specifying include_groups=True in DataFrameGroupBy.apply() and Resampler.apply()
candidates.note: Portable: use d.name inside the function.
candidates.old:
df = pd.DataFrame({'g': ['x', 'x', 'y'], 'v': [1, 2, 3]})
r = df.groupby('g').apply(lambda d: d['g'].iloc[0])
assert r.tolist() == ['x', 'y']
candidates.new:
df = pd.DataFrame({'g': ['x', 'x', 'y'], 'v': [1, 2, 3]})
r = df.groupby('g').apply(lambda d: d['v'].sum(), include_groups=False)
assert r.tolist() == [3, 3]

outcome.new@old: error: TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'include_groups'

candidates.description: inplace=True returns self instead of None.
candidates.quote: Methods that can operate in-place ... now return the modified DataFrame or Series (self) instead of None when inplace=True.
candidates.note: The natural old form (call, then use df) works in both.
candidates.old:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1.0, np.nan]})
assert df.fillna(0, inplace=True) is None
candidates.new:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1.0, np.nan]})
assert df.fillna(0, inplace=True).sum().sum() == 1.0

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError
outcome.new@old: error: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'sum'

candidates.quote: Now it performs inference on the appropriate resolution
candidates.note: New capability; the natural old form is portable.

r = pd.to_datetime(['1500-01-01'], errors='coerce')
assert r.isna().all()
candidates.new: assert pd.to_datetime(['1500-01-01']).year[0] == 1500

assert s.dtype == object
s[0] = 1
assert s[0] == 1
candidates.new:

assert s.dtype == 'str'

candidates.quote: Enforced deprecation of strings T, L, U, and N denoting units in Timedelta

candidates.new: assert pd.Timedelta(5, unit='min').total_seconds() == 300

candidates.description: errors='ignore' removed from to_numeric/to_datetime/to_timedelta.
candidates.quote: Removed support for errors="ignore" in to_datetime(), to_timedelta() and to_numeric()
candidates.old:
r = pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(['1', 'x']), errors='ignore')
assert r.tolist() == ['1', 'x']
candidates.new:
r = pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(['1', 'x']), errors='coerce')
assert r.isna().tolist() == [False, True]

candidates.description: Copy-on-Write: chained assignment no longer updates the frame.
candidates.quote: Because every single indexing step now behaves as a copy, this also means that "chained assignment" ... will stop working.
candidates.new:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2, 3], 'b': [4, 5, 6]})
df.loc[df['b'] > 4, 'a'] = 0
assert df['a'].tolist() == [1, 0, 0]

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError

candidates.description: Reductions no longer drop non-numeric columns silently.
candidates.quote: Changed default of numeric_only to False in all DataFrame methods with that argument
candidates.old:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2], 'b': ['x', 'y']})
assert df.mean()['a'] == 1.5
candidates.new:
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2], 'b': ['x', 'y']})
assert df.mean(numeric_only=True)['a'] == 1.5

outcome.old@new: error: TypeError: Cannot perform reduction 'mean' with string dtype

candidates.description: np.array(copy=False) now means never copy; copy=None is the new spelling of copy-if-needed.
candidates.quote: The meaning of False changed as it now raises an exception if a copy is needed.
candidates.note: 1.26 rejects copy=None ('NoneType copy mode not allowed'); portable: np.asarray(x).
candidates.old:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], copy=False)
assert a.tolist() == [1, 2, 3]
candidates.new:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], copy=None)
assert a.tolist() == [1, 2, 3]
b = np.asarray(a, copy=None)
assert b is a

outcome.old@new: error: For more details, see https://numpy.org/devdocs/numpy_2_0_migration_guide.html#adapting-to-chan
outcome.new@old: error: ValueError: NoneType copy mode not allowed.

candidates.description: floor/ceil/trunc keep integer dtypes.
candidates.quote: numpy.floor, numpy.ceil, and numpy.trunc now won't perform casting to a floating dtype for integer and boolean dtype input arrays.
candidates.note: Natural tasks are portable in one direction.
candidates.old:
r = np.floor(np.array([1, 2, 3]))
r[0] = np.nan
assert np.isnan(r[0])
candidates.new:
i = np.floor(np.array([0, 2]))
v = np.arange(5)[i]
assert v.tolist() == [0, 2]

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to integer
outcome.new@old: error: IndexError: arrays used as indices must be of integer (or boolean) type

candidates.description: loadtxt/genfromtxt encoding default bytes -> None: converters get str, not bytes.
candidates.quote: loadtxt and genfromtxt now both default to encoding=None which may mainly modify how converters work. These will now be passed str rather than bytes.
candidates.note: Portable: encoding='utf-8' with a str converter. Both failures surface as ValueError.
candidates.old:
import io
conv = lambda b: float(b.replace(b',', b'.'))
r = np.loadtxt(io.StringIO('1,5;2,0'), delimiter=';', converters={0: conv, 1: conv})
assert r.tolist() == [1.5, 2.0]
candidates.new:
import io
conv = lambda s: float(s.replace(',', '.'))
r = np.loadtxt(io.StringIO('1,5;2,0'), delimiter=';', converters={0: conv, 1: conv})
assert r.tolist() == [1.5, 2.0]

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: could not convert string '1,5' to float64 at row 0, column 1.
outcome.new@old: error: ValueError: could not convert string '1,5' to float64 at row 0, column 1.

candidates.description: unique(return_inverse=True) keeps the input shape for n-D input; np.unique_inverse is new.
candidates.quote: the unique_inverse output is now shaped such that the input can be reconstructed directly using np.take(unique, unique_inverse) when axis=None
candidates.note: Portable: ravel the inverse.
candidates.old:
a = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 3]])
u, inv = np.unique(a, return_inverse=True)
counts = np.bincount(inv)
assert counts.tolist() == [1, 2, 1]
candidates.new:
a = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 3]])
codes = np.unique_inverse(a).inverse_indices
assert codes.shape == (2, 2)

outcome.old@new: error: ValueError: object too deep for desired array
outcome.new@old: error: AttributeError: module 'numpy' has no attribute 'unique_inverse'

candidates.description: String to bool casts test non-emptiness instead of parsing ints.
candidates.quote: Now a string of "0" will be considered True since it is not empty.
candidates.old:
flags = np.array(['0', '1', '1']).astype(bool)
assert flags.tolist() == [False, True, True]
candidates.new:
flags = np.array(['yes', '', 'no']).astype(bool)
assert flags.tolist() == [True, False, True]

outcome.old@new: error: AssertionError
outcome.new@old: error: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'yes'

candidates.description: A trailing comma in a dtype string makes a structured dtype.
candidates.quote: a trailing comma will now always create a structured dtype
candidates.note: Contrived as a task.
candidates.old:
a = np.zeros(3, dtype='i8,')
b = a + 1
assert b.tolist() == [1, 1, 1]
candidates.new:
a = np.zeros(3, dtype='i8,')
col = a['f0']
assert col.tolist() == [0, 0, 0]

outcome.new@old: error: IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices

candidates.description: copyto/full casting no longer looks at values.
candidates.quote: np.coptyo(int8_arr, np.int64(100), casting="safe") raises. Previously, NumPy checked whether the 100 fits the int8_arr.
candidates.note: Contrived as a task.
candidates.old:
a = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int8)
np.copyto(a, np.int64(100), casting='safe')
assert a.tolist() == [100, 100, 100]
candidates.new:
f = np.zeros(2, dtype=np.float32)
np.copyto(f, 1e300, casting='safe')

candidates.description: NEP 50 promotion: Python scalars are weak; no value-based promotion.
candidates.quote: np.float32(3) + 3. now returns a float32 when it previously returned a float64.
candidates.note: Splits into two one-directional tasks, one per direction.

b = a + 300
assert b.dtype == np.uint16 and b.tolist() == [500, 550]
candidates.new:

assert x.dtype == np.float32

candidates.description: np.sign of complex numbers is z/|z|.
candidates.quote: the complex sign is now calculated as z / |z|

candidates.description: any/all on object arrays return booleans.
candidates.quote: The any and all functions and methods now return booleans also for object arrays.

candidates.description: float()/int() on a size-1 array with ndim > 0 raises.
candidates.quote: Conversion of an array with ndim > 0 to a scalar was deprecated in NumPy 1.25. Now, attempting to do so raises TypeError.

candidates.description: count_nonzero(axis=None) returns a NumPy scalar.
